title: Mitochondrial oxidative DNA damage and exposure to particulate air pollution in mother-newborn pairs.
ehr_evidence: We recruited mother-newborn pairs (only singletons) in the East-Limburg Hospital in Genk, Belgium who are part of the ongoing birth cohort “ENVIRONAGE”.
summary: Prospective birth cohort study assessing the association between prenatal particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) exposure and mitochondrial oxidative DNA damage (8-OHdG) in maternal and cord blood.
key_findings: PM10 exposure during the entire pregnancy was associated with an 18.3% (95% CI: 5.6 to 33.4%, p=0.004) increase in maternal mitochondrial 8-OHdG.
PM10 exposure during the third trimester was associated with a 28.1% (95% CI: 8.6 to 51.2%, p=0.004) increase in maternal 8-OHdG.
PM2.5 exposure during the entire pregnancy was associated with a 13.9% (95% CI: 0.4 to 29.4%, p=0.04) increase in maternal 8-OHdG.
PM2.5 exposure during the third trimester was associated with a 28.1% (95% CI: 3.6 to 58.4%, p=0.02) increase in maternal 8-OHdG.
PM10 exposure during the first and second trimesters was associated with 23.0% (95% CI: 5.9 to 42.8%, p=0.007) and 16.6% (95% CI: 1.8 to 33.5%, p=0.03) increases in cord blood 8-OHdG, respectively.
No significant association was found between PM exposure and cord blood 8-OHdG during the entire pregnancy (p>0.11).
High 8-OHdG levels correlated with high mtDNA content in maternal (r=0.44, p<0.0001) and cord blood (r=0.58, p<0.0001).
No association was found between PM exposure or 8-OHdG levels and birth weight or small for gestational age.
population: 293 pregnant women and their newborns from the ENVIRONAGE birth cohort in Genk, Belgium
limitations: Mitochondrial 8-OHdG measured only at end of pregnancy, limiting assessment of changes during gestation.
Potential residual confounding by unknown factors.
Exposure estimated via spatial interpolation rather than personal monitoring.
No significant associations found with adverse pregnancy outcomes like birth weight.
